newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia deploys troops on Madura before re-vote.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia deploys troops on Madura before re-vote.

text.p: Indonesia has deployed at least 3,000 troops on Madura island ahead of a re-vote after riots sparked by the ruling Golkar party's sweeping general election victory last week, police said on Monday.
The General Election Commission will hold a re-vote at two locations on Madura, off the East Java coast, on Tuesday after ballot boxes were destroyed following the elections last Thursday.
"We have deployed around 3,000 troops on the island to counter violence, especially because there will be a re-vote...," East Java police spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Sofwat Hadi said.
Angry Moslems started rioting on Thursday night following the elections and violence continued through the weekend.

Golkar took more than 74 percent of the national vote, with the Moslem-backed United Development Party (PPP) winning almost 23 percent after an election campaign that saw the worst political violence in the country in three decades.
The only other party permitted to contest the poll, the badly fragmented Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), slumped to three percent.
The PPP said on Monday it had instructed party branches through the country to report to police and prepare lawsuits against local election officials over alleged election fraud.

"The instruction dated May 31 is made because of the many reports coming to the PPP's central executive board about various cheatings, either during the voting day or during the vote counting," it said in a statement.
It gave no details and PPP officials could not be reached for comment. Party officials earlier said they would meet next Thursday to decide whether to accept the election result.

Golkar chairman Harmoko on Sunday rejected charges by an independent watchdog set up by activists and government critics that there were systematic violations of electoral laws and vote rigging in favour of Golkar.

Diplomatic analysts said Golkar had brought its big guns to bear on East and Central Java -- where it suffered a drop in support in the last elections in 1992 -- largely at the expense of the PDI. Top Golkar leaders, including President Suharto's eldest daughter, pushed the party's cause in the regions.
Its share of the votes in East Java, which includes Madura, rose to 63 percent in Thursday's poll from 59 percent in 1992, while the PDI's share plummeted to three percent from 16.
In Central Java, it shot up to 68 percent from 55.4 percent, while the PDI slumped to 2.7 percent from 22 percent.
The PDI was decimated following a leadership struggle in which popular leader Megawati Sukarnoputri, daughter of Indonesia's founding president Sukarno, was ousted by a government-backed faction.
The East Java police spokesman said stern action would be taken against rioters in future.
"There will be no compromise," said Hadi, adding that Madura was generally calm on Monday.

Thousands of people rioted on Thursday night, burning houses, offices and a church, alleging vote rigging after Golkar appeared to be sweeping the election on Madura. Violence continued into Sunday morning.

In the former Portuguese colony of East Timor at least 34 people, including 16 policemen and two soldiers, were killed over a four-day period in violence related to separatist attempts to disrupt the polls, police said.
